title: Residents vote on the upgrading budget
issue: Has letting residents vote on the budget led to better decisions for the estate?
background:
A town council set aside $500,000 of its yearly improvement budget for residents to decide. Residents proposed projects. Every household could then vote, online or at a booth beside the market, over two weeks in March.

The three projects with the most votes were built: a covered walkway, a fitness corner and a new playground. About one in seven households voted. The council is now deciding whether to hold the vote again next year with a bigger sum.

Study the sources to find out whether letting residents vote has led to better decisions for the estate.

sources.provenance: A poster by the town council, put up at lift lobbies before the vote.
sources.text:
Your estate. Your say.
This year YOU decide how $500,000 is spent.
Propose a project. Vote for three. Every household has one vote.
The projects with the most votes will be built. It is that simple.
Voting is open 1–14 March, online or at the booth beside the market.

sources.provenance: A resident who proposed the covered walkway, speaking at a residents' meeting after the results were announced.
sources.text: For six years we asked for a covered walkway from Block 214 to the bus stop. Nothing happened. This time we knocked on doors, got our neighbours to vote, and it came first. For once the people who use the path decided, not an office that has never walked it in the rain.

sources.provenance: A letter from an elderly resident to the town council, a month after the vote.
sources.text: I am 78 and I do not use a smartphone. I learnt about the vote only when I saw workmen at the playground. The booth was at the market for two weeks, but nobody told us at Block 230. The blocks with young families and big chat groups got what they wanted. Our broken ramp, which wheelchair users need every day, got 41 votes and nothing.

sources.provenance: From the town council's yearly report to residents, published three months after the vote.
sources.text: The budget vote was a great success. 2,140 households took part, far more than attend our meetings in a whole year. All three winning projects were completed on time and within budget. Residents have told us they feel heard. We plan to double the sum next year.

sources.provenance: From a study by university researchers, who surveyed 600 households in the estate after the vote.
sources.text: One in seven households voted. Among households with children, one in four voted; among residents aged 70 and above, one in twenty. The three winning projects were all within 300 metres of the blocks that voted most. Yet 68% of those surveyed, including many who did not vote, said the vote was a fairer way to decide than before. Most asked for paper voting forms next time.

sources.provenance: An engineer who works for the town council, interviewed for a community newsletter.
sources.text: The walkway and the fitness corner are well used. But the vote cannot see everything. The ramp at Block 230 and the old water pipes under Block 208 are urgent, and they will never win a popularity contest. If all the budget went to a vote, the things nobody notices until they fail would be left out. A vote is good for choosing between nice things, not for deciding what is necessary.

title: Raising the price of water
issue: Was raising the price of water the right decision?
background:
The national water agency raised the price of water by 20% in two steps, the first on 1 July. It was the first rise in twelve years. The agency said that water now costs more to produce, because more of it comes from treating sea water and used water.

Households in smaller flats were given rebates on their bills. Shops, stalls and factories paid the new price in full. Some people welcomed the rise as a way to make everyone save water. Others said it was unfair.

Study the sources to find out whether raising the price of water was the right decision.

sources.provenance: A poster by the national water agency, put up at bus stops in the month before the first rise.
sources.text:
Every drop costs more to make.
Twelve years ago, most of our water fell from the sky. Today more of it must be made from the sea, and that takes four times the energy.
The price of water has not changed in twelve years. From 1 July it will.
For most families the rise is less than the price of one cup of coffee a week.
Use a little less, and you may pay no more than before.
Rebates are on the way for smaller flats.

sources.provenance: The owner of a noodle stall at a hawker centre, interviewed by a newspaper a week after the rise was announced.
sources.text: I use water all day to boil noodles and wash bowls. My bill will go up by about $60 a month. I cannot use less water. A clean stall needs water. The rebates are for households, not for stalls. So I either raise the price of a bowl by 20 cents or earn less. Many of my customers are retired and count every coin. People say the rise is small. It is small for an office, not for me.

sources.provenance: A letter to a newspaper from a mother of three who lives in a two-room flat, a month after the first rise.
sources.text: I was angry when I heard the news. Then I looked at my bill. With the rebate my family pays about $3 more a month. That I can manage. And the rise did make us change. My children now take shorter showers, and we mop the floor with the rinse water from the washing machine. But I worry about my neighbour, who lives alone. Nobody told her about the rebate in a language she reads. She is so afraid of the bill that she now washes her clothes by hand, once a week.

sources.provenance: A ministry spokesperson, speaking at a public forum six months after the first rise.
sources.text: The rise has worked. In the six months since July, households used 4% less water per person. That is the biggest drop in ten years. Nine in ten households in smaller flats received rebates that covered most of the rise. No family has had its water cut off because of the new price. We know nobody likes to pay more. But the money is building the pipes and plants that our children will depend on.

sources.provenance: From a report by university researchers, who studied the water bills of 800 households, published eight months after the first rise.
sources.text: Households used 4% less water per person in the first six months. But the fall was uneven. Households in large flats and houses cut their use by 1%. Households in one-room and two-room flats cut by 9%, and one in five of these said they now flush or wash less often than they think is healthy. Most households could not say what the new price was. Households that received a letter comparing their use with that of their neighbours cut more than those that only paid the higher price.

sources.provenance: An online post by an environment group, in the week the rise was announced.
sources.text: At last. For twelve years water was priced as if it would never run out. A person here uses about 140 litres a day, and a long shower is cheaper than a bus ride. When something is cheap, people waste it. A higher price is the only message that reaches every home at the same time. We ask only that the heaviest users pay the most, so that those who fill swimming pools pay more for each litre than those who fill a kettle.

title: Closing a neighbourhood school with few pupils
issue: Is closing the school the best choice for its pupils?
background:
A primary school in an old estate had 1,200 pupils twenty years ago. Today it has 310, because fewer young families live nearby. The ministry has announced that the school will merge with a bigger school 2 kilometres away at the start of next year. The old building will close.

Every pupil has been given a place at the bigger school, and a free bus will run for the first two years. Parents, teachers and former pupils have spoken up, some for the merger and some against it.

Study the sources to find out whether closing the school is the best choice for its pupils.

sources.provenance: An online petition started by former pupils of the school, in the week the merger was announced.
sources.text:
Save our school.
For 58 years this school has been the heart of the estate. Our parents studied here. We studied here.
A school is not a shop that closes when it has fewer customers.
Small classes mean every teacher knows every child by name. That is worth more than a bigger hall.
Sign before 30 April and tell the ministry: fill the school, do not close it.

sources.provenance: A ministry spokesperson, speaking to parents at a meeting in the school hall after the merger was announced.
sources.text: With only 310 pupils, the school can offer just four after-school activities, and it has one class at some levels. A child who falls out with classmates cannot move to another class. Some teachers must teach subjects they were not trained for. At the bigger school, your children will choose from 19 activities, with a new science room and a trained teacher for every subject. Every pupil has a place there. A free bus will run for two years. We are not closing a school. We are giving its pupils more.

sources.provenance: A parent of a Primary 3 pupil at the school, writing in an online forum for parents the day after the meeting.
sources.text: My son walks to school in five minutes with his grandmother. From next year it is a bus at 6.30 in the morning. And what happens when the free bus stops after two years? He is a quiet boy. In a class of 24 his teacher noticed in one week that he could not see the board. In a class of 40, who will notice? They talk about 19 activities. I did not choose this school for activities. I chose it because he is known here.

sources.provenance: A teacher at the school, interviewed for a community newsletter.
sources.text: I love this school, and I will cry on the last day. But I must be honest. I teach English, and for two years I have also taught music, which I never studied. Last year we could not form a football team because too few boys signed up. Our pupils do well because the classes are small, yet they also miss out. What worries me is the move itself. The children who struggle most are the ones who find change hardest, and nobody has yet told us how many of our teachers will go with them.

sources.provenance: From a study by university researchers of pupils whose schools had merged in earlier years.
sources.text: We followed 450 pupils from three schools that merged between five and eight years ago. After two years, their test results were about the same as before the merger. Nine in ten said they had made new friends, and seven in ten joined an activity their old school did not have. However, in the first year, absences rose among pupils who lived more than 2 kilometres from the new school, and one in four pupils from low-income homes said they often felt left out. Results were better where teachers from the old school moved together with their pupils.

sources.provenance: A letter to a newspaper from a parent whose child went through an earlier school merger, written in the week the merger was announced.
sources.text: Three years ago the school my daughter attended merged with a bigger one. She cried for a week. I was one of the parents who signed the petition against it. I was wrong. In her old school she was the only girl who liked chess. In the new one she found a chess club and eight friends who play. Her class is bigger, but two teachers take it for mathematics. The journey is 15 minutes longer. She would not go back.

title: Second-hand smoke between neighbouring flats
issue: Is a law the best way to protect neighbours from second-hand smoke?
background:
Smoking is not allowed in many public places, but people may smoke inside their own flats. When a person smokes at a window or balcony, the smoke can drift into the flats above and beside. Complaints about this have grown.

At present, a resident who is troubled by smoke is advised to speak to the neighbour, and then to ask for mediation, where a trained helper guides both sides to an agreement. Some residents want a law against smoking at windows and balconies. In May, a ministry asked the public for views.

sources.text:
Your home. Their smoke.
Every night, smoke from the flat below comes through our windows. We close them. We buy fans. Our children still cough.
Talking has failed. Three in four of us who asked a neighbour to stop saw no change.
There are rules against noise after 10.30 p.m. There are none against smoke at any hour.
The ministry is asking for public views until 31 May. Write in. Ask for a law that keeps smoke out of our homes.

sources.provenance: A letter from a resident to the town council.
sources.text: My son is six and has asthma. The neighbour downstairs smokes at the window from 9 p.m. until past midnight, and the smoke rises straight into the room where my son sleeps. I asked politely twice. The second time the neighbour said it is his home and his right. Your officer came, gave him a leaflet and told me there was nothing more to be done because no rule was broken. We now sleep with every window shut. Please do not tell me again to talk to my neighbour.

sources.text: I have smoked for thirty years and I know it is bad for me. I cannot smoke at the coffee shop, the void deck, the park or the bus stop. My flat is the last place left. I smoke at the window so that my wife and grandchildren do not breathe it. When my neighbour upstairs told me the smoke reached her flat, I moved to the kitchen window on the other side, and I now stop by 9 p.m. That took one conversation. A law would send officers to watch windows and turn neighbours into informers. Ask first.

sources.provenance: A ministry spokesperson, replying to questions from residents at a public forum in May.
sources.text: A law must be one we can enforce. To prove that a person smoked at a window, an officer would have to watch or film a private home. Few residents would want that. Smoke also drifts from doors and kitchens, which a law on windows would not cover. Mediation works: seven in ten cases that reach our community mediation centres end with an agreement. We will keep helping neighbours to settle these matters with good sense. A law is the last tool, not the first.

sources.text: One household in four said that smoke from a neighbour entered their home at least once a week. Of those who asked for mediation, only one case in five went ahead, because both sides must agree to attend. Where mediation did take place, seven in ten cases ended with an agreement. title: Sharing the void deck for different events
issue: Have the new booking rules helped residents share the void deck fairly?
background:
The void deck of a block of flats is shared by everyone who lives there. Families of different races and religions use it for weddings, funeral wakes, prayers and festival meals. Sometimes two families want the same space, or neighbours are upset by noise.

In June, a town council brought in new rules for one estate. Residents book the void deck online or at the office. Each booking is posted at the lift lobby three days ahead. Music must stop at 10 pm. title: Mixing households of different races in each block
issue: Has the rule that mixes races in every block been good for residents?
background:
Most people in Singapore live in public flats. Since 1989, a rule has set a limit on the share of flats in each block and each neighbourhood that households of one race may own. When a limit is reached, an owner may sell only to a buyer whose race will not push the share higher.

The rule is meant to stop any estate from becoming home to one race only, and to let neighbours of different races meet in daily life. Some owners say it makes their flats harder to sell. In 2024, residents of one estate were asked what they thought of the rule.

Look down your corridor.
One neighbour hangs lanterns for the Mid-Autumn Festival. Another lights oil lamps for Deepavali. A third brings round kuih for Hari Raya.
This did not happen by chance. In every block, families of every race live side by side, because the rule keeps it so.
Different doors. One corridor. That is home.

sources.provenance: A letter from a flat owner to the housing authority, written in 2024 after selling a flat in the estate.
sources.text: I put my flat up for sale last March. The limit for buyers of my own race had been reached in my block, so most of the families who came to view could not buy it. After nine months I sold to the only buyer allowed, for $38,000 less than a neighbour two floors up got the year before. My children grew up with friends of every race on this floor, and I am glad of it. But the whole country gains from mixed blocks, while the cost fell on my family alone.

sources.text: When I worked night shifts, the family next door took my son in after school every day. They are of a different race and religion from us. They never once gave him food he could not eat. Today my son and their daughter still meet for supper. If we had all lived among our own kind, I would have known them only as faces on a bus. Some people say the rule is a burden. For me it was the best thing that happened to this family.

sources.text: The rule has served residents well for more than thirty years. Every block in this estate is home to families of all races. Residents get along, and most residents tell us they are comfortable with neighbours of another race. Only a very small number of sellers are affected by the limits, and any of them may appeal. The rule does not hold back prices. We see no reason to change it.

sources.text: 86% of households said they were comfortable having neighbours of another race, and 71% greet such a neighbour most days. But only 22% had shared a meal with one in the past year. One block in three had reached a limit. In those blocks, flats took about four months longer to sell and went for about 5% less. Even so, 64% of the owners in those blocks said the rule should stay.

title: Help by community groups or by income alone
issue: Are needy families better helped by community groups than by one scheme based on income alone?
background:
In Singapore, several self-help groups each serve one ethnic community. Working adults give a small sum from their pay each month to the group for their community. The groups run low-cost tuition, give bursaries and help families in difficulty.

Supporters say a group that shares the language and customs of a family can reach it more easily. Others ask whether help should depend only on income, with one scheme for everyone. In March 2024, a committee of citizens began hearings on the question. It heard from the groups, from families and from researchers.

Study the sources to find out whether needy families are better helped by community groups than by one scheme based on income alone.

sources.provenance: An advertisement by a community self-help group, placed in a community newspaper in March 2024, the month the committee began its hearings.
sources.text:
When a father of three lost his job, the family did not need a form explained. They needed someone who spoke their mother tongue, who knew why they would not ask relatives for money, and who would sit with the children at homework time.
We are not an office. We are your own community, and we know our families.
The committee is now asking whether groups like ours are still needed. Tell them. Write in by 30 April. Better still, come and volunteer on Saturdays.

sources.provenance: A social worker at a family service centre that serves residents of all races, interviewed for a news website.
sources.text: Hardship does not check your race. A family that cannot pay the rent needs the same things, whoever they are. I have seen two neighbours with the same income get very different help, because one group had more donors than the other. I have also met families who stayed away from their own group because they were shy of being seen by people they know. The volunteers in these groups work hard and I respect them. But one door for everyone, opened by need alone, would be simpler and fairer.

sources.provenance: A parent whose children were tutored by a community self-help group, speaking at a hearing of the committee.
sources.text: When my husband fell ill, I rang a national hotline and was sent a list of forms. Then a volunteer from our community group came to the flat, spoke to my mother in our own language and found my son a tutor within the week. The tutor grew up poor in this same estate. My son listened because here was someone like us who had made it. I know a smaller group may have less to give, and that is not right. Fix that. But do not take away the people who knew how to reach us.

sources.provenance: From a study by university researchers, who followed 800 pupils from low-income families for three years.
sources.text: Pupils tutored at a centre run by a community group attended 85% of their classes. Pupils at centres open to all attended 70%. Parents told us they trusted volunteers who shared their language. But the largest group spent about $520 a year on each pupil it helped, and the smallest about $290. One in five low-income families had never approached any group. Marks in mathematics rose by about the same amount at both kinds of centre.

sources.provenance: From a joint statement by several community self-help groups, sent to the committee and to newspapers in April 2024.
sources.text: Our groups reach families that no single office could. Every family that needs help can get it from its own community, in its own language. No community is left behind, because each group gives its pupils the same support. Parents trust us, and our pupils attend far more regularly than pupils elsewhere. issue: Have the dialect classes helped the young stay close to their elders and their heritage?
background:
Many older Chinese Singaporeans grew up speaking a dialect such as Hokkien, Teochew or Cantonese. Since the late 1970s, Mandarin has been encouraged as the common language among Chinese Singaporeans. Most children today speak English and Mandarin, and many cannot speak the dialect of their grandparents.

In 2023, a community club in one estate began free Saturday dialect classes for children aged 7 to 14. The teachers are volunteers, many of them retired. In the first year, 120 children joined. The club must now decide whether to pay for the classes for another year.

title: A festival street closure and the shops nearby

title: Paid enrichment classes and a free tuition scheme

title: A foreign chain opens where local shops stood

title: A car-free town centre on weekends
issue: Has closing the town centre to cars on weekends been good for the town?
background:
Market Street runs through the middle of Riverside town centre. It is lined with shops, cafes and a hawker centre. On weekends it used to be packed with cars looking for parking.

This year the town council closed Market Street to cars every Saturday and Sunday for a six-month trial. Buses stop at both ends of the street, and a free shuttle bus runs from two car parks. The council will soon decide whether to keep the car-free weekends.

Come on the first weekend and see your town centre in a new way.

title: An online petition to save an old playground

background:

Once the ship is gone, it is gone for ever.
If you grew up here, played here or brought your own children here, sign below and share this page.
We will hand every name to the town council before it decides on 30 June.

title: Making first-aid training compulsory for secondary pupils
issue: Has the compulsory first-aid course prepared pupils to help in an emergency?
background:
Last year a secondary school made a first-aid course compulsory for all its Sec 3 pupils. The course takes six Saturday mornings. Pupils learn how to treat cuts and burns, how to do CPR on a practice dummy, and where the school keeps its heart-starting machine. The school pays a training company to run it.

Before this, pupils could join a first-aid club if they wished. About one pupil in ten did. The school is now deciding whether to keep the course compulsory next year.

Study the sources to find out whether the compulsory course has prepared pupils to help in an emergency.

sources.text:
Be the one who helps.
This year every Sec 3 pupil will complete a first-aid course over six Saturday mornings.
You will learn to stop bleeding, treat burns and do CPR.
An emergency can happen at home, on the bus or on the field. When it does, the people nearby are the first help that arrives.
Attendance is compulsory. A certificate will be given to every pupil who completes the course.

sources.provenance: A blog post by a Sec 3 pupil at the school, near the end of last year.
sources.text: I was annoyed to lose six Saturday mornings. But last month my little cousin cut her hand badly on a broken cup at a family dinner. Everyone panicked. I pressed a clean cloth on it and held her hand up, like we practised. My aunt said I was calmer than the adults. I still do not think I could do CPR on a real person. But at least I did not freeze.

sources.provenance: A letter from the parent of a Sec 3 pupil, printed in the school newsletter.

A month later he could not tell me the steps of CPR. First aid is a useful skill, and I would gladly pay for a small class. But a big compulsory course where most pupils just watch is not the way to teach it.

title: Signs in four languages at a new community centre
issue: Have signs in four languages made the new community centre easier for everyone to use?
background:
A new community centre opened three months ago in an older estate, next to the wet market. It replaced a small centre that had signs in English only.

Every sign in the new centre is in four languages: English, Chinese, Malay and Tamil. Big signs in the lobby point to the hall, the clinic and the lifts. Small signs on each door name the room. The centre runs free classes for older residents, such as exercise and cooking.

Study the sources to find out whether signs in four languages have made the community centre easier for everyone to use.

sources.provenance: A speech by the chairman of the management committee of the community centre, at its opening ceremony.
sources.text: Welcome to your new community centre. When you walk in, you will see that every sign here is in English, Chinese, Malay and Tamil. That was our choice. Many of our older residents grew up reading only one of these languages. We do not want any of them to stand at the door feeling this place is not for them. So please, tell your parents and grandparents: come in, look around and join a class. This centre was built for all of us.

sources.provenance: A letter to the community centre from a young man, written for his grandmother, who reads only Tamil.
sources.text: My grandmother is 78. She reads only Tamil. At the old centre she never went in alone, because she could not tell which room was which. Last week she took the lift to the exercise class by herself, following the signs. She was so proud that she told the whole family at dinner. She says the signs make her feel that she belongs there too. Thank you for thinking of people like her.

sources.provenance: An online post by a young mother who lives in the estate, two months after the centre opened.
sources.text: I like the idea of signs in four languages, but the small signs are now too crowded to read. On the door of each room there are four lines of tiny print. Last Saturday my son needed the toilet, and I walked past it twice. Simple pictures, like a toilet or a lift, would help everyone, whatever language they read. Bigger print would help older eyes too.

sources.provenance: From the newsletter of the community centre, sent to every home in the estate three months after it opened.
sources.text: Our signs in four languages have been a great success. Older residents tell us they no longer feel lost. 1,200 residents aged over 60 have joined our classes, twice as many as at the old centre. A sign in your own language says that this place is yours. Join a class this month and bring a neighbour.

sources.provenance: From a survey by a group of university students, who asked 300 users of the centre how they found their way, three months after it opened.
sources.text: Of users over 60, 6 in 10 said they read the signs in their own language at least sometimes. Most said they still asked the staff at the front desk. 4 in 10 said the print on the small signs was too small to read. Among younger users, most read only the English line. When asked why they joined a class, most older users said it was because the centre is next to the market and the classes are free. Only a few named the signs.

sources.provenance: A front desk officer at the community centre, interviewed by a newspaper three months after it opened.
sources.text: At the old centre, older residents came to my desk all day to ask where to go. Here, fewer people ask about the main rooms, like the hall and the clinic. The big signs work. The small signs on each door do not. With four languages on one small plate, the letters are tiny. Many older residents also cannot read well in any language, so a sign does not help them. For them, a friendly face at the desk is still the best sign.

title: A new dormitory for migrant workers near an estate
issue: Have the new dormitory and the housing estate become good neighbours?
background:
Many of the workers who build homes, roads and train lines in Singapore come from other countries. Most of them live in dormitories.

A year ago a new dormitory for 800 workers opened on empty land beside a housing estate of 12 blocks. Before it opened, some residents asked for a meeting about the road and the bus stop that the dormitory would share with the estate. The company that runs the dormitory has held open days for residents.

Dear neighbours,
A dormitory for 800 workers will open on the empty land beside Block 12 next year. We are not against the workers. They build our homes, and they deserve a good place to live.
But nobody has told us how 800 more people will share our one small road and our one bus stop. Buses will come and go at dawn.
Please come to our meeting at the void deck of Block 9 on Friday at 8 pm. Let us ask for a plan that works for everyone.

sources.text: My last dormitory was two hours by lorry from my work site. Here it is 30 minutes, so I sleep more. We are eight to a room, not sixteen, and the kitchen is clean. On Sundays I play cricket on the field with some boys from the estate. They are getting good. Some residents smile and say hello at the bus stop. Some cross the road when they see us in a group. I understand. They do not know us yet.

sources.text: Every morning at six, two big buses wait under my window with their engines running, to take the workers to their sites. The noise wakes me every day. That is a problem with the planning, not with the workers. The workers themselves are polite. Last month one of them carried my shopping up from the market when the lift was broken. I would like the town council to move the buses inside the dormitory gate.

sources.text: Our dormitory has shown that workers and residents can be good neighbours. Our workers and the residents of the estate now mix freely at our open days. Every worry raised before we opened has been solved. We listened, and we moved the morning buses inside our gate. We are proud of this dormitory, and we are ready to build more like it in other towns.

sources.provenance: From a study by researchers at a university, who questioned 400 households in the estate and 200 workers in the dormitory, a year after it opened.
sources.text: Most households said the dormitory had changed their daily life very little. The most common complaint was the noise of buses at dawn. Most workers said they felt welcome in the shops of the estate. Few had a friend there. Both groups said they would like more chances to meet.

Neighbours Day

title: Older residents and a skate park in one estate

background:

Soon some older residents complained about the noise and about near misses on the path. The council then set quiet hours: no skating before 9 am. Every few years, smoke from fires in a neighbouring country drifts here. Many of the fires are lit to clear land for farms, including farms that grow oil palms. Palm oil is used in many foods and soaps sold in our shops.

This year the haze lasted three weeks. On the worst days the air was unhealthy to breathe. Schools kept pupils indoors, and clinics saw more people with coughs and asthma.

People here cannot put out fires in another country. Some say there is still a lot they can do. Others are not so sure.

Study the sources to find out how much people here can do about the haze.

sources.text: Haze is back this week. Here is what we are doing for you. Free masks for every resident aged 65 and above, at the community centre from Monday. Air purifiers have been placed in all eight senior corners at our void decks. Keep windows closed, check on elderly neighbours, and stay indoors if you feel unwell. We cannot stop the smoke, but together we can look after one another.

sources.provenance: A letter to a newspaper from a mother whose son has asthma, written during the haze.
sources.text: My son has asthma. This week he has used his inhaler more times than in the whole of last month. We keep every window shut and stay in. Telling us to wear masks and stay indoors is not an answer. The fires are lit in another country, by people who will never read our posts. Signing petitions and checking labels will not stop them either. Nothing we do here reaches the people who light the fires. Every year we wait for the wind to change.

sources.text: Did you know that many everyday goods, from biscuits to shampoo, contain palm oil? Some of it comes from land cleared by fire. sources.text: We asked 800 shoppers about the haze and palm oil. Nine in ten said they were angry about the haze. Seven in ten said they would choose goods made without burning. But when we checked the till records of three supermarkets, goods with a no-burning label made up fewer than 1 in 20 of the items sold that had palm oil in them. Most shoppers said they could not find the label, or that labelled goods cost more.

sources.provenance: A speech by the head of a palm oil trading company, at a business conference here a month after the haze.
sources.text: Our company buys palm oil from hundreds of small farmers in the region. We have told every one of them that we will not buy oil from land cleared by fire. Since we made this rule, demand from shoppers here for clean oil has grown fast, and we now pay farmers more for it. The haze is a problem for all of us. Business and shoppers are already solving it together.

sources.provenance: A scientist who studies air quality at a university, interviewed on a radio programme during the haze.
sources.text: The smoke comes from fires hundreds of kilometres away. No mask or purifier here changes that. Only the governments of the region, working together, and the companies that own the land can stop the burning. But what people here do still matters at the edges. Buyers who refuse oil from burnt land give companies a reason to change. That pressure works slowly, over years, not in one haze season. Meanwhile, the most useful thing people here can do is protect the old and the sick.

Many young people here hope to work overseas for a few years. Most of them already speak English and their mother tongue.

More of them are now learning a third language, such as Japanese, Spanish or Korean. Private language schools offer holiday courses. One secondary school plans to offer a third language to all its Sec 3 pupils next year. Learning a language well takes years, and pupils must give up time for other things.

Some say a third language opens doors abroad. Others say skills and work experience matter more.

Study the sources to find out whether learning a third language is the best way to get a job abroad.

title: Self-checkout machines replace cashiers at a supermarket
issue: Have self-checkout machines been good for everyone at the supermarket?
background:
A supermarket chain here has 40 shops. Two years ago it began replacing most of its cashier counters with self-checkout machines. The machines are made overseas and are used by supermarkets in many countries. Shoppers scan their own goods and pay by card, phone or cash. A few staff stand nearby to help.

The chain had about 400 cashiers. Some were moved to other jobs in the shops. Others left. The chain plans to put machines in all its shops by next year.

sources.text: I worked at the counter for 14 years. I knew the regulars by name. When the machines came, I was offered a job stacking shelves on the night shift. Now I go to the small shop near my block, even though it costs more. Machines are for the young.

title: World coffee prices and the neighbourhood coffee shop
issue: Is the rise in world coffee bean prices the main reason coffee at the coffee shop costs more?
background:
Coffee beans are grown in hot countries far away. Last year bad weather ruined the harvest in several of them, and the world price of coffee beans almost doubled.

In an older estate, a drinks stall in the neighbourhood coffee shop has sold kopi for 20 years. In March it raised the price of a cup of kopi from $1.40 to $1.80. Many regulars were unhappy. In the same year, the rent for stalls in the coffee shop also went up.

sources.text: Dear customers, from 1 March kopi and teh will cost 40 cents more. We kept our prices the same for three years. Coffee beans now cost us almost twice as much as last year, because of bad harvests overseas. We are sorry. We still roast our beans the old way every morning, and we will not switch to cheaper beans. Thank you for drinking with us for 20 years.

From now on I will make my coffee at home.

sources.provenance: From a study by researchers at a university, who looked at the costs of 60 drinks stalls in older estates.
sources.text: Over the past year, the cost of the beans in one cup of kopi rose by about 10 cents on average. Rent and wages together added about 8 cents a cup.
